newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - Rodeo cowboys take danger in stride.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Rodeo cowboys take danger in stride.

text.p: Huge bucking bulls have briefly paralysed Tuff Hedeman and broken every bone across the centre of his face.

But the 33-year-old rodeo rider refuses to dwell on those injuries, or on a herniated disc or countless other broken bones and strained muscles suffered over the last 15 years, as he prepares to climb onto "Gold Dust," a 2,000-pound (900 kg) bull, for a wild eight-second ride.

"You have to block the danger out of your mind. If you get on worrying about injury and getting hurt that's exactly what is going to happen," said Hedeman, a three-time world champion bull rider on the grueling professional rodeo circuit.
Carefully adjusting his cowboy hat before climbing aboard at a recent rodeo in Fort Worth, he said caution can prove costly or even fatal in one of the world's most dangerous sports.

"Whatever you do, you can't ride them careful. You've got to be aggressive, give it everything you've got, or you're in deep trouble," he said with a smile twisted by reconstructive surgery that followed a 1995 accident in which he fell forward and cracked his face on the bull's head as it bucked backwards.

In 1993, a bull tossed and kicked him, paralysing him for 15 minutes. Hedeman also suffered a herniated disc in that spill and was convinced it was the end of his career, but he healed quickly and had no hesitation in returning to the ring. "This is what I do, I'm a rodeo cowboy," he said simply.
Others have not been so lucky.

Blaine Manigold was recovering from an earlier back injury when he jumped off a bull at the end of a successful ride in July 1995. As he hit the ground, the bull kicked out to the side and caught him in the back, fracturing his fifth and sixth cervical vertebrae and damaging his spinal cord.
ACCIDENT LEFT HIM PARALYSED

"It left me pretty much without muscle use from the collarbone down. I have very little feeling," the wheelchair-bound Manigold said at his home in Stephenville, Texas, where he is trying to rebuild his life by studying physical rehabilitation and sports at college.

He said nobody ever explained to him the full dangers of riding with a weakened back but insisted he had no regrets. "I did what I did because I loved it. There is no point in being negative, it's just one of those things that happen," he said.
"I still miss it, all the travelling and talking with my buddies. I loved the competition and the camaraderie with all the guys. I just miss the lifestyle."
The professional rodeo circuit averages one or two deaths per year, most of them in bull riding, and hundreds of injuries ranging from sprained wrists to serious spinal and brain damage.

Joint injuries are common to all riders but each event has its typical dangers. Calf roping and steer wrestling commonly cause hand, wrist and shoulder injuries, while saddle bronc and bareback riders are at risk of serious neck and back injuries caused by whiplash, falling from the horse and being kicked.

Bull riders face all of the above and can also be jumped on or caught by the bull's horns. Most fatalities are caused by the bull stomping on the rider's head or neck as he falls to the ground. Others suffer facial fractures and head wounds by falling onto the bull's tossing head and horns.
But few regard the bulls, which weigh up to 2,200 pounds (1,000 kg), as enemies because a rider's score depends not only on technique but also on how well and hard the bull bucks.
THE BULL IS A PARTNER
"It's almost like the bull is your partner," Manigold said. "The toughest bull in the pen is the one you want because he is going to make you look good and hopefully win you some money."

Rodeo fans see the danger, and the way riders face up to it, as a key element of the sport's appeal, a testament to the competitors' toughness and dedication. "Those cowboys either love it to the core or they're just plain crazy. I haven't figured out which it is yet," said anaesthesiologist Dr. Grady Carter, part of the medical emergency back-up team at the Fort Worth rodeo.

He said he once treated a bareback rider who asked him to reset a dislocated shoulder on the spot rather than waste time by sending him to a hospital. "I pulled his shoulder out, dragged it across and pushed it back in. He never whined a word, looked straight at me and said, 'Thank you.' I tell you, these guys are the toughest athletes alive."

While the top rodeo stars can earn upwards of $100,000 a year in prize money and as much again in sponsorships, most riders make only a modest living after paying for travel and entrance fees and earn nothing at all if they cannot compete.
Economic necessity and a passion for their trade push some riders into ignoring their injuries or rushing back to compete before they are properly healed.

More and more riders have begun using protective jackets over the last five years but, in a sport unrivalled for its macho credentials, almost all of them frown on suggestions that they wear helmets instead of their beloved cowboy hats.

"It just wouldn't look right, or feel right. It would take some of the mystique away," said Bob Logue, a bareback rider who suffered a "hangman's fracture" to four vertebrae in 1983 when a horse fell on him, pushing his body back over his head.
While rodeo doctors say they are concerned that riders take too many risks they clearly admire their patients.

"I'd rather take care of a guy who wants to push it than someone who is happy sitting on his butt," said Tandy Freeman, an orthopedic surgeon with the Justin Sportsmedicine network of physicians, which provides special care to rodeo cowboys.

Freeman treats professional basketball and other sports stars but said rodeo riders are his favourite. "They never walk out of here without saying 'Thank you.' That doesn't happen much in pro sports, but it's just the cowboy way."
